analysis.one_liner: Bans selling or sharing people's personal data without their express consent, and lets people sue violators.
analysis.headline: The Personal Data Privacy Act of 1998 never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to a House committee and a subcommittee in August 1998 and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred government agencies and private companies from transferring, selling, or disclosing any individually identifiable personal data — names, addresses, Social Security numbers, medical records, credit card accounts, school records — without the person's express consent, with narrow exceptions for national security, law enforcement, and regulatory purposes [S2][S3]. It would also have required agencies and companies to let people see their own data within five business days of asking and to send everyone an annual report of what data was collected on them [S2][S3]. People whose data was mishandled could sue in federal court [S3]. The bill was introduced late in the two-year session with no cosponsors and never moved past its first committee referral [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose identifying information — Social Security numbers, medical records, driver's license numbers, credit card accounts, school records, internet addresses — is held by businesses and government agencies. Everyone would gain the right to refuse consent before their data is sold or handed to another entity, to see their own file within five business days of asking, to get a yearly accounting of what was collected on them, and to sue when the rules were broken [S2][S3]. The law would have covered federal, state, and local agencies as well as private companies [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose personal data is collected

how_it_helps.text: No government agency or private business could sell, transfer, or disclose individually identifiable data about a person — including Social Security numbers, medical records, credit card accounts, and school records — without that person's express consent, except for national security, law enforcement, or industry-regulation purposes [S2][S3].

People could demand access to the personal data an agency or company holds on them within five business days, and would automatically receive an annual report listing everything collected on them in the prior year [S2][S3].

The bill included a private right of action, so a person whose data was sold or shared without consent could take the violator to federal court rather than relying on a government agency to enforce the rules [S3].
The rules covered every level of government — federal, state, and local — plus any business, corporation, joint venture, affiliate, or subsidiary, closing the most obvious loopholes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, credit bureaus, financial companies, marketers, and any business whose revenue depends on collecting and reselling customer information would lose the ability to trade in personal data without consent. Government agencies would bear new paperwork duties — five-day access responses and annual individual reports — and could face lawsuits for violations [S3].

drawbacks.text: The exceptions were broad: government agencies could still share personal data for any purpose 'relating to the Federal or State regulation of an industry,' a carve-out wide enough to swallow much of the restriction for agency-to-agency transfers [S3].

The compliance burden was heavy and immediate: every covered entity had to answer data-access requests within five business days and send an annual report to every person it held data on, and the bill was set to take effect less than three months after introduction, on November 1, 1998 — a timeline businesses and agencies would have found difficult to meet [S3].

The bill reached no one in Congress but its sponsor: it had zero cosponsors, was introduced with less than five months left in the session, and received no hearing, markup, or floor action, so it was never debated on its merits [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — nobody sells your Social Security number, medical records, or credit data without asking you first — is a real benefit to ordinary people, and the private right of action gave it teeth that many later privacy laws lack. The trade-offs are real but manageable: the regulatory-purpose exception was loose, and the five-day access and annual-report requirements would have been costly for large companies and agencies, especially with the effective date set before the bill could even have passed. On balance the benefits to individuals outweighed those compliance costs, but the bill was so late in the session and had so little support that its design was never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee and then to a subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on August 6, 1998, with less than five months remaining in the 105th Congress [S1][S5].
No members signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Government Reform and Oversight the day it was introduced [S5].
Eleven days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology, where it stayed [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action is recorded before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that profit from collecting, reselling, and sharing personal data — and government agencies that trade in it — kept operating without a consent requirement, and no one had to comply with the five-day access or annual reporting rules.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough engagement to reveal a partisan split: it had one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever taken on it.

industries.note: Their entire business is collecting and reselling identifiable personal information; the bill's blanket consent requirement would have shut down sales and transfers without permission, and the private right of action would have exposed them to suits.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: Credit card and account data is explicitly listed as 'personal data' in the bill, so compiling and selling credit files would have required consumer consent each time.

Banks and card issuers could no longer share customer account information with outside entities without consent, restricting a revenue stream, though they would still hold and use their own customer data.

The bill would have imposed real compliance duties — five-day data access, annual reports to individuals, litigation exposure — but carved out national security, law enforcement, and industry-regulation purposes, preserving most of the government's ability to share data among itself.

School records, student IDs, and employee-related identifiers fall within 'personal data,' so routine record-keeping and referrals would have needed consent, adding cost but also giving individuals control over their own files.
